THE B I B L I
P S I U
By Peter A.
In 1882,' fifty-nine years ago, Willard Fiske, Psi '51, published his
"Bibliographia Psiupsilonica," a 17page booklet dealing With the 58
volumes of memorabilia" at the Chi
Chapter, and described by Albert
Poole Jacobs in his Epitome of 1884.
During the six decades which have
elapsed, a
steady growth of the Fra
ternity has occurred, and a vast store
of bibliography has 'accumulated,
some of which has already been noted
in the fore-pages of the Annals of Psi
Upsilon.
In presenting this two-column
format, we shall follow the current
method of the New York Public Li
brary, and shall describe briefly the
bibliography of Psi Upsilon from the
beginning.

ven, 1842. The catalogues and their

Prepared and issued by William E.
Robinson, Beta '41, assisted by a
Coinmittee of the Beta. Listing 243

EIGHTH CATALOGUE OF 1870. Listing
3525 names of the 15 Chapters. In
Four Years at Yale the catalogue was

ever issued by a
college society. 233
pp. By Committee of the Beta, Rob

NINTH CATALOGUE OF MARCH 1879.
Listing 4940 names of the 17 ChapSI UPSILON
ters. Contained 467 pp. being more
than twice as
many as the Eighth.
Charles W. Smiley, Xi '74, Editor.
Under authority of Executive Coun
cil. Published at New York.
Governor Alexander H. Rice, Theta
'44, in his introduction to the Cata
logue wrote: "The present volume ap
pears under the modest title of a
'Catalogue of the Psi Upsilon Frater
nity', but a
glance at its comprehen
sive plan wUl indicate that it might
with equal propriety be styled a bio
graphical and statistical record of its
members. As such, it is beheved to
be unique and marks a new
departure
in the practice of Greek Letter So
cieties."
The New York World editorially
wrote: "A monumental cataloguewhen a
graduate's affection for his
college societies leads him to devote
two solid years of his life to prepar
ing a record of its membership ac
cording to an ideal standard of excel
lence which no man has ever had the
courage to adopt ... it is to say that
it is a
unique achievement and, there
fore, wordiy of at least the degree of
attention due by common consent to
every literary novelty."
From The Scroll of Phi Delta
Theta, November 1884: "The pubfication of the catalogue of Psi Upsilon
in 1879 caused a revolution in the art
of catalogue making. This superb
work was
regarded with astonish
ment
by the Fraternity World. It not
only far surpassed all previous efforts
of the kind, but it remains as a
standard by which to compare all
subsequent catalogues."

History of Psi Upsilon of

CHAPTER LISTS. Aside from the Cata
logues which have been published by
the Fraternity, many chapters and
alumni associations have published
chapter lists. For example, in 1902,
the Chi produced an
alphabetical list
of members consisting of 32 pp. The
Omicron of 1910 likewise prepared an
attractive book, as did the Rho in
1912 which contained 40 pp.
ALUMNI AND CLUB DIRECTORIES. The
alumni of Detroit, Boston, Washing731

ANNALS OF PSI UPSILON
ton, Chicago, Cleveland and others
have produced directories, with one
of the finest being prepared by A.
Avery Hallock, Xi '16, for the Cleve
land Club in 1921. It was a
garnetbound book, 96 pp. of which 15 are
devoted to songs. Most of these books
were
prepared for the vest pocket and
measure 3 x 6 in.
A fine example of a sustained effort
to produce Directories was that of
the Psi U. Club of New York, which
prepared a booklet of 22 pp. in Janu
ary 1887, carrying constitution, by
laws, house and visitors' rules and list
of members. It had a
garnet-enamel
paper cover which was 5% x 4M in. It
produced other Directories in 1888,
1892, 1894, 1895, 1897, 1900, 1905.
In 1909, the book consisted of 47
pp., with a
garnet cover, SVa x 7 in.,
which style it continued in 1912,
1915, 1916. In 1917, it produced an
Honor Roll of 20 pp. of those who
were
participating in the World
War, a booklet 3M x 5% in. In 1931,
the Directory contained 47 pp.,
goldenrod-paper cover, 6M x 5 in.
The Psi Upsilon Club of Chicago,
1940, published a
43-pp. Directory,
one of the finest examples of club
catalogues, giving oflBcers, calendar
of events, membership, classified Hsts
as to chapters, and support of indi
viduals who underwrote the pubKcation.
THE SONGS OF THE
FRATERNITY
The First Song Book was issued in
1849. The Epitome of Albert P. Jacobs
reported, as of 1884, that, "No copies
are known to have survived the lapse
of time, but old graduates recollect
the existence of the work. It seems to
have been a httle affair of 8 pp. con
taining 8 songs." Willard Fiske, in
his "Bibliographia Psiupsilonica," of
1882, reports no
knowledge of the
title of our First Song Book. How
ever, he opened the song section of
his Bibliography with the following
famihar song, which also appears on
the title page of the First Song Booh

TENTH EDTTioN, 1891. This book was
copyrighted by the Executive Coun

Xi '82. The Editor in his preface
wrote: "During the decade that has
now
elapsed since the last edition of
this song book, much progress has
been made in the improvement of
college singing and many new Psi U.
songs have been written on various
occasions. As a result, the Tenth Edi

presents a number of novel features.
It contains 186 songs, of which 88
have never
appeared in any previous
edition, 82 new tunes are included
within its covers. Of these new
acqui

pieces of music composed expressly
for this edition mostly on
especial
sohcitation."
The Brooklyn Standard Union,
December 12, 1891, devoted a column
to the Tenth Song Book and said in
part: "The first Psi Upsilon Song Book
was a
pamphlet of 16 pages, pub
lished in 1849, and containing no mu
sic, and the evolution of the present
book of 256 pages is a
fitting Hlustration of the strength and progress of
this foremost of college Greek Letter
Societies. Psi Upsilon has always been
renowned for its songs and singing,
and the new
song book demonstrates
that this fame is deserved and so be
maintained." Published in Philadel
phia. 9M X 7)8 in. 256 pp.

SONG BOOKLETS. Almost without ex
ception every important Psi Upsilon
function has been accompanied with
a booklet of songs. Usually they con
tain the national favorites, chapter
songs and sometimes popular college
songs. To describe the varying char
acter of these booklets would require
a
separate chapter. They have been
grand or
simple, many pages, or
just
a few songs interleaved in a
banquet
program. The Executive Council for
many years and now the Alumni As
sociation of Psi Upsilon supplies a
booklet of 25 pp. containing reprints
of the words of songs from the official
Song Book for use at banquets and
reunions.

following expresses the general tenor
of all. "Throughout its history. The
Diamond has been a labor of love by
a
procession of devoted Psi Upsilons.
While many have labored on The
Diamond and have tasted the joy of
labor well and lovingly done, yet I
fancy all will be eager to join in these
tributes to Brother Corcoran, who, as
Business Manager, and then as Edi
tor, and always as
generalissimo, has
been the leading spirit in the success
ful revival of The Diamond. Possibly
without him, and certainly without
the kind of service he has rendered,
it would have been an
impossible
task."
